props.title: The Evil Dead
props.initialSlug: Five friends face demonic terror in remote cabin

sections.content: **The Evil Dead** (1981) revolutionized low-budget horror with Sam Raimi's kinetic camerawork and Bruce Campbell's iconic performance as Ash Williams. Shot for just $375,000, the film's innovative POV shots, extreme gore effects, and that relentless "demon-cam" rushing through the woods influenced countless horror films. Raimi's creative solutions - like mounting the camera to a 2x4 for tracking shots - showed aspiring filmmakers how to achieve professional results on a shoestring. The cabin-in-the-woods setup became a horror template, directly inspiring works like **Cabin in the Woods** (2011) and **Tucker & Dale vs Evil** (2010).

sections.content: The original spawned an entire "cabin horror" subgenre. **Friday the 13th Part 2** (1981) capitalized on isolated woodland terror, while **The Cabin in the Woods** (2011) cleverly deconstructed these tropes. The film's practical effects by Tom Sullivan - particularly the decomposing Deadites and stop-motion animations - influenced a generation of horror effects artists. Modern films like **The Void** (2016) and **Terrifier** (2016) carry on this practical effects tradition. SUBHEAD: Impact on Modern Horror

Raimi's dynamic visual style reverberates through contemporary horror. **Don't Breathe** (2016) and **Drag Me to Hell** (2009) showcase his influence on camera movement and tension-building. The original's blend of horror and dark humor paved the way for films like **Dead Alive** (1992) and **Re-Animator** (1985). Modern filmmakers like James Wan (**The Conjuring** [2013]) and Mike Flanagan (**Doctor Sleep** [2019]) have cited The Evil Dead as a major influence on their approach to supernatural horror.
